of The Covenant of the

paras.text:
What you hold in your hands is the
present translation of his work from High into Common Imperial, a project which
began with the Karshbaum rendition of CP 798, and ended with the Thompson &
Gonzalez revision of CP 803. This undertaking corrects numerous errors of idiom
and cultural context by translating directly from the source documents.
However,

Readers should be aware that
certain terms resist translation altogether. The Chronicler's use of the word kephale, for example, carries a connotation of "source" not observed in
contemporary Common. Similar simplifications are found in the handling of
Kifune honorifics, where higher ranks are flattened into the generic "elder." The deeper nuances of High Imperial, itself
rooted in 20th Century English, fall beyond the scope of this edition.

paras.text:
The division of the text into
chapters is by design, though a small number of titles were appended by later
copyists for the purpose of distinguishing certain passages from their adjacent
material. Dated in the Third Century of Paradise, they are thus preserved, but
noted where they occur.

This edition preserves the
Chronicler's account in its fullness, inclusive of those passages which strain
credulity and those which, by the Committee's estimation, achieve a beauty that
transcends the question of their accuracy. We commend it to the reader as neither gospel nor fable, but as the labor of a man who loved the subjects of his
writing and told their story as faithfully as his nature allowed.

paras.text: PREFACE
I suppose I should explain myself.

What follows is a testimony of the High Council of the
Realm, and the final days of her Founders. Even more so, it is the story of her
children, tasked with settling the balances that remained, and what became of
the world when they did. I
cannot claim to be unbiased, and where the urge for soliloquy has tempted me, I
confess I did not try very hard to resist it. Should you find my telling
over-exuberant at times, I do not hold this critique against you.

It is important to note that I did not witness these events
firsthand. I arrived too late for that, as I do most things. But I have spent
the better part of my life in the company of what they left behind. Letters,
journals, the fading memories of old men and women who were young when their
own grandparents spoke of an era too remarkable to be true.

Ah, but I already
grow excessive, scribbling as though the Realm were ancient history. Someday
this manuscript will be far older than I can presently imagine, in a century I
cannot guess, and someone will have to decide whether anything I’ve said ever
happened at all.

I picture this person sometimes. A fellow scholar of
Citadel, perhaps, discerning whether they hold a gift or a curse in what I’ve
left behind. Self-indulgent as it may be, I wonder what word they will use for
it.
I suspect the word will be myth.
paras.html: I suspect the word will be myth.

paras.text:
Which is a strange word, on consideration. A word for a
story we no longer feel obligated to believe, but are unwilling to forget. We
say of certain old tales that they are only myths.
paras.html: Which is a strange word, on consideration. A word for a story we no longer feel obligated to believe, but are unwilling to forget. We say of certain old tales that they are only myths.

paras.text:
And yet we keep them. We pass them to our children. We
carve them upon our buildings. A culture that truly believed its history untrue
would not bother.

So when I imagine that future scholar deciding what I have
written is myth, I am not certain whether to be aggrieved or relieved.
Aggrieved, because the people I write about were not invented for the
edification of the young. Relieved, because a smaller word would disservice them.
Perhaps it only matters that we remember.

This work has
taken me longer than I intended. Now that it stands complete, it has robbed me
of my halcyon days, most of my sanity, and the one person I most wish could
read it. If she were here, she would tell me this story was worth waiting for
anyway.

She’d
be right.

May
the Eight-Point Endure Eternal.
PROLOGUE

A gentle breeze carried the smell of
dew and progress while tall flags swayed proudly upon the first completed towers
of a home for many. From where the two men stood, cliffside fell into terraced
hills and the makings of a great Babylonian garden. Across the estuary, water broke the evening into pieces and
threw them up at the towers, which passed the light between their faces, glass
to glass, until the whole waterfront glittered. All
around them, their city rose in exposed steel, cranes reaching above those with
unfinished crowns.

Andrew shielded his eyes from the edge
of the overlook. Beside him, Jeff ran a hand over airy curves and patterns in
the banister. His sleeves were still rolled up, with flecks of limestone along
his arms.
“Think they’ll come?” he asked.

Andrew watched a construction lift
descend the open side of the trade center, carrying the last of its crew toward
its central lobby. “Eventually,” he said. “If we hold to our vision.”

Jeff nodded, then leaned on the rail.
They were men still in their early twenties, one with dangerous eyes, the other
a dangerous smile.

“Feels uncanny, doesn’t it? That we’re
actually doing it. That it’s coming to pass.”

Andrew glanced over. “Little late to
be getting cold feet, coward.”

“Weren’t you struggling to get down
that ladder earlier?” Jeff sniped. “I’m just surprised no one’s told us to stop
yet.”

Andrew turned back toward last light,
his own palms now on the banister. “They will. For now, we’ll let them scratch
their heads. As long as we puzzle it all out before they do.”

They laughed, and for the moment, the
world felt right. Contractors in a mess tent belting lyrics in their native
tongues, a wheelbarrow tipping over in the gravel, followed by a muffled curse
and a man throwing his hard hat down to punctuate his wit’s end. There was much to do, but it was
theirs, born from dreams they’d sworn to each other long before the first
cornerstone was laid.

“And you believe it will last?” Jeff
asked. “When the roads are green, and no one remembers what it took to get
here, will our vision be carried forward?”

Andrew shrugged. “Our job isn’t to
decide whether men walk the roads we pave. Our job is simply to pave them.”

Jeff pondered that for a moment. Then
he reached into his coat and pulled out a scrap of folded parchment. Handed it
over.
“What’s this?”

“The list. People we talked about
bringing in.”

Andrew looked at the paper, then out
at the rising beams below. “Uncanny how alike you and Mark think sometimes.”

Jeff made a gesture of caution.
“Before we drag anyone else into this, let’s make a pact. Just us, like old
times.”

He was sounding like a younger version
of himself, before he was a magnate of the old company. How good it was to
remember those days, and their bond that had carried them all this way, through
the years of doubt and struggle. Even now, they were standing here not by
contracts or titles, but in bindings of faith, in shared dreams of a world
remade.
“I’m listening.”

Jeff looked him in the eye. “We finish
what we started. No matter how big it gets, no matter who tries to tear it
down. We build this for our children and their children. And we don’t let the
world scare us out of it.”

Andrew threw an arm around his closest
friend, one of the precious few he’d ever called brother, and the one for whom
he’d come to lay down his life. They looked out on the night horizon, at the
wide unknown.

“Together,” he said, sealing this
permanence with that dangerous smile.

So it was, dear reader, that the
vision born beneath unfinished archways took root in the hearts of many. What
began as a skeleton of concrete and steel became the heart of the Atlantic, a center
of trade and innovation, of treaty and charter. These men and women were the
very breath of the Realm, a stretch of land once fractured by feuding nations
and lesser ambition, now held in balance by a Council of their making. Others
stood among them, and together, they fashioned law from wisdom, order from
will. And the Realm prospered.

Then, in the third year of peace, they
discovered the existence of a leyline flowing beneath the land, pulsing with a
melody too sublime for nature alone. It led them across the sea, through
mountain and forest, to the secret gates of Kifune. And whether by chance or by
invitation, they were granted entrance.

It was there the great question was
answered, and the Fount chose to be known. It was there the covenants were
struck, the terms of which are the task of this chronicle to bear witness. It
was there the season of light began.

This is not the story of such days.
This is the story of things that came after that golden memory, when the long
dusk began.
ACT ONE
I
The Eight-Point Chrysanthemum

There are no true beginnings in
history. This is the struggle of my profession, for where on the continuum of
history does a chronicler place his finger that leaves no missing context, no
heroes unsung?

And yet I must choose a morning, for
the alternative is to choose no morning, and in such a world, you and I are
never given this time together.

So. Let us step back nearly two
centuries, to the fifth Cycle of Paradise. It is a hot afternoon. There is a
small shop in a dying town, and a visitor in the sophomore years of her
girlhood approaches. We shall witness her put on a performance of sophistication
despite being largely kept from the world, but we shall not judge her too
harshly, for we were once young ourselves.

A small bell sounded at the corner of
the doorway, and in she walked.

She brushed dust from her cowl,
keeping her face within its shade while her eyes adjusted from the glare
outside. In the dimness, the shelves were little more than dark shapes at
first, but gradually she made out lines of books, and glass jars, and an older
man behind the counter, murder weapon still in hand—for the music he made with
it had struck her down in the street.

He glanced up, his bow finishing its
run before he lowered it.
“A fine day to you, madam.”

“I heard your violin,” she said. “And
found myself lured inside. It spoke to me of impermanence, as though each note
were remembering a lost home far away. Such profound melody, master bard. A
rarity in these days of paradise, I must say.”

He returned the instrument to its
case, latching it closed. “If only it were on younger strings and quality
rosin. Perhaps you’ll find our wares as worthy of attention.”

Her hand dithered over them as she
browsed, a habit that had been called maddening by many a merchant, though this
man seemed immune to it. A spool of textile took her breath away, and then a
sewing kit took it instead, and then something else.

“The smell of varnish tells me you’ve
done all you can to preserve their beauty. Let not these trying times trouble
you. Mr. Bodecker?”
“That’s me.”

A risk-free guess, by the sign
outside: Bodecker’s Curiosities and Ciphers.

“Might I buy a glass of water? I’d pay
handsomely, if you’ve any to spare.”

The shopkeeper glanced toward the
window, an ire on his brow. She wondered whether she’d asked too much, when he
reached beneath the counter and brought up a decanter and glass.
“I take it the truck is late again?”

A rhetorical question, so she did not
answer it. He drew the stopper from its decanter, but before he could pour, she
placed an iridescent silver talent upon the counter. The petals of the
Eight-Point Chrysanthemum were as certain as if they were freshly minted.

Few elements compared to the rarity of
selenic silver—pound for pound—though this was not the cause for his low
whistle. He set the decanter down.

“Did someone send you shopping with
that?”

Until this morning, the talent had
been stashed at home with a hundred others just like it, where her uncle seemed
content to forget them. Perhaps he’d have preferred she ask before helping
herself to his money, but she’d felt it only considerate to minimize the
explanations and discussions that would come attached. To spare them both.

But why should her good fortune
trouble this Mr. Bodecker? Was her charade so legible from across the counter?
Would he suspect her thievery and call the guards? She could invent a name,
perhaps even an explanation, but she could hardly invent another face.

“I’m just here on business, master
bard.”

His expression offered little
assurance, but the tilt of the decanter offered plenty. He pushed the glass
toward her, but as she reached for it, his fingers tightened about its base,
drawing it back. “First, your cowl. I don’t do business with those I can’t look
in the eye.”

Her uncle had fashioned it for
those occasions when necessity brought them into the city, along with a veil to guard
against recognition as much as to protect against the Pox. If his precautions
were any indication, being her parents’ daughter was something the Empire might
hold against her, and on that account she was to remain inconspicuous and leave
the talking to him. This policy was still in place. Now she was beginning to
understand why.

“Surely my etiquette has been
introduction enough,” she said, despairing at the glass now out of reach. “Does
my compensation not afford me a measure of anonymity?”

“You’re asking for more discretion
than you seem to realize.” He glanced at the coin, then back to her. “If I’m to
accept what you’ve placed on the counter, I’d like to see whom I’m dealing
with.”
“And if I decline?”
“Then we haven’t made a purchase.”

Whatever had startled him lay there
upon the counter, and she ought to have gathered it and been on her way, to be
forgotten as shadows are forgotten. But she remembered the truth of his violin,
in their shared culture, their homeland, their music. As much as this, she
wanted him to be pleased in what he saw, pleased to have her at his door. Her
intuition had already co-signed the risk, and she unfastened the cord that held her veil secure.
“Only for a moment,” she said.

She slipped the veil beneath her chin.
Her fingers ran along the inner edge of her hood before she drew it down about
her neck, feeling the air against her ears.
“See me truly.”
His hand loosened about the glass.

There are faces which return the dead
to us without warning. Harry Bodecker had known her father’s, and now Andrew’s
daughter stood across his counter, trying very hard to look as though she’d
surrendered nothing of consequence.
“Extraordinary.”
“Have I satisfied you?”

“Yes.” He pushed the glass within her
reach. “Forgive me.”

She brought it to her lips, meaning to
take a mouthful, then finding it difficult to stop. The sweetness flooded her
senses and her eyes closed of their own accord.

For it was a time of great thirst in
the region—a curse, it was suspected, which was why the drought had come to be
known as the Writ of the Land. And while the period may seem a modest length
for those of us who may know it through a turn of the page, for her it was a
dry, crunchy tome a lifetime in the reading.

When she opened her eyes, he was still
looking at her.
“Do you recognize me, Mr. Bodecker?”

“You’ve grown,” he said. “Though I
recognize your mother and father both. I wouldn’t have expected to find so much
of them together in one face.” His eyes moved to the window, where the chatter
of two passersby carried through. “Your veil, child. You were right to keep it
up.”

She drew it about herself before
raising her cowl, watching him all the while.

She’d guessed right, but it seemed
she’d gotten more than she’d bargained for. The work of her parents had
remained largely a mystery. She remembered a certain degree of privilege, the ease with which her father entered meetings regardless of an invitation.
What any of it meant had scarcely concerned her then. Now someone stood before
her who might be willing to explain it. Or was it a wound too deep for him to
address, as it was for her uncle?

“I recall very little of them now,”
she said. “I’d barely lost my baby teeth when…”

At her uneven breath, Mr. Bodecker
shook his head. “You may be proud of them. Whatever anyone else has told you.
Your father stood tall. Even at the end.”

Then he began to prepare her change.
“Now is hardly the time or the place to reminisce about the glory days. Let us
take care not to invite further danger to my door.”
“I understand,” she said.

Bodecker laid out her change in legal
tender: a stack of crowns and several pennies wearing the likeness of Imperator
Dämmerung. Beneath his silhouette ran the inscription Pax Paradisi. That
is to say, Peace of Paradise.

paras.text:
“Dapper,” remarked Bodecker. “Isn’t
he?”

“I hold no opinion on the matter. But
why are these so unlike the money I gave you?”

“Because the coin you brought is
Realm-relic. It was supposed to be exchanged when the imperial money came in,
long enough ago that the wardens stopped accepting excuses. I hope you haven’t
been flashing it around.”

Her eyes went from the counter to its
keeper with new clarity of her misjudgment. “Then I ought to take it back.
Surely I’ve put you at risk!”

“You’ve bought a glass of water.” He
nudged the crowns toward her. “Take them.”

Her ears grew warm at the unmasking of
her ignorance, and she gathered the money with an air of displeasure. “You
won’t give it back, then. Fine.”

“It’s for your own good, child—and the
good of whichever poor fool you stole it from. Hey now, there’s no need to
cry.”

“I’m not even upset.” Lie. “I just
loved your violin playing.” Truth.

And are we all not a little guilty of
this? Speaking around a feeling until we find a morsel we can bear to offer:
{The music was beautiful.
The day was hot.
We are merely tired.}

These may be true, and serve us well
enough, until those wiser have no choice but to save us from ourselves. Then we
must trust our saviors with what we cannot quite bring ourselves to say: think
kindly of me; allow me a little dignity while I recover.

To Harry Bodecker fell the commission
of wisdom.
“I’m glad you came in,” said he.

The girl stopped just short of the
door, her hand never making it to the handle. A modest shop, a glass of water,
and a pinch of grace: these were sufficient materials, as is always the case
when the Fount has provisioned.

She turned. “Might I come again, then?
At a more suitable hour?”

Despite having counseled restraint, he
permitted himself a modest exception. “Old Fire’s Day is nearly upon us.
Perhaps its eve, after I close.”

That old Realm holiday. She’d almost
forgotten it. “And should I bring something?”

“If you like. As I recall, I’d heard
tell of the youth favoring a more extravagant observance.” His eyes wandered
somewhere far away, somewhere long ago. 
“There are still a few sentimental old fools who prefer to keep it to a
candle at the table.”

He smiled, his eyes finding her again.
“Or so I’m told. You understand, I’ve no particular love for dead traditions
myself.”

“Your indifference is magnificently
unconvincing, bard. Nevertheless, I might be convinced of it—once we’ve
reenacted this forgotten custom. Purely out of historical interest, of course.”
“Then I shall be expecting you, milady.”

“Until then,” she said, laying an
admonishing index finger against her lips.

He bowed his head, and the bell
sounded as she let herself out.

The heat found her instantly, and she
fanned herself while keeping to the shade. The market throng was a din of
withered faces and sweat-stiffened tunics, bound to the province by a
stubbornness that had outlasted its canals for longer than she could remember.
And yet even the natives would have since departed if not for imperial charity.

Only this relief kept the city going;
water and produce entering over roads that had once carried the harvests away.
With the city spiraling in debt, the government had seen fit to waive taxation
and other administrative nuisances.

These were things she needed to learn
more about, if she wanted to stay alive. The money she swiped from home could
have undone everything, but why had Mark been squirreling the talents all this
time, rather than ridding himself of their indictment? He owed her an
explanation, one she intended to have.

A tremor shook the air, rattling
everything not bolted down. Around her, people were haggling, hawking their
wares, mouths still moving through sentences she could no longer hear over the
roar above.

She shielded her eyes as she raised
them.

Two Corsair Novas streaked through the
sky toward Testament. They flew so high that she could have hidden both behind
her thumb, sunlight glinting off their underbellies as they banked. Then the
spacecraft were gone from sight, and the peal of their Einherjar engines soon
after.

She found she was not the only one to
follow their wake. Some paces away, a peculiar fellow kept his blue-gray eyes
fixed on the sky. She guessed him a little older than herself.
“Loud,” she offered.

The stranger lowered his gaze until he
found her. “Empire’s never been known for its subtlety, to be fair.”

“Well,” the girl replied, “a little
restraint would be welcome.”

Now that he faced her, she could see
how badly his hair wanted clipping. It curled over his ears and fell across one
eye, obliging him to brush it aside, and there was something alluring about the
way he did.

“I’ll mention it next time I’m in
Citadel.”

The girl weighed the likely
possibility she was being teased, though he seemed willing to await her
judgment on the matter. “See that you do.”

He grinned, then checked beneath the
neighboring stall.

A stray hound lay in the shade, chin
resting on a dusty paw. At the sight of him, her tail beat against the
pavement. He knelt as she struggled up to greet him, ribs hard not to notice
beneath her coat, nose fast in his palm.

“There’s our princess. I missed you
too, pretty girl.”

He fetched his flask, unscrewed its
cup, and poured a little water for her to drink. As he did, the girl came a few
steps nearer, moved by how readily he shared what little he had.
“Is she yours?”

“She’s her own. I look in when I can.”
He gave her a familiar pat as she lapped, his hair falling across the leanness
of his face. There was a strength to him that didn’t register at the start. A
curious sort, the girl thought. She grew increasingly studious of his
frame, such that she barely heard herself ask his name.

paras.text:
At the question he looked up in
surprise. Few now bothered to know such things.
“Evan,” he told her.
“Well. Goodbye, Evan.”

She crouched to give the dog a parting
scratch behind the ear. When she straightened, the young man was already
halfway through the market and approaching the southside bridge. Not even a
parting word?

She set off in the same direction,
halted by a vendor wheeling his trolley through the junction. Once the path was
clear, her sandals earned their keep without complaint, enduring every stomp a
young man's lack of decorum deserved.

“Are you following me?” he asked, not
looking back.

“Do I need permission to cross a
bridge? I shall not take the long way home merely to deny you an inflated
notion of yourself.”

The young man shortened his stride
until she drew level, and they proceeded in tandem. “If our way is the same,
this would be less awkward,” he said.

“Agreed. But do not readily assume
companionship, sir. You will have better luck with the girls at Citadel.” Hmph!

Masterfully played, for Citadel lay at
the heart of Crown City, and Crown City lay conveniently on the far side of the
Atlantic. She had sent him an ocean away in search of more interested parties,
without surrendering her place beside him.

Not that she had any real impression
of the world capital—beyond a few memories she’d long since buried—but surely
it was much the same as here.

And here was a town well west of the
Appalachian ridges, bordered by mills and silos worked by none save the
grasshoppers. Commodities came east and west by rail, water brought from a
dying lake named Erie. Cartographers after the Dämmerung Era had taken to
calling the town Historia, though her original name remains uncertain.

Dämmerung. The first true khan, the
high chieftain of every tribe, binding all beneath his banner. Not an inch of
earth remained outside his dominion, which is why—as our textbooks teach us—the
man and the peace became one and the same.

But the textbooks always refrained
from taking aim at the heart, which was the part she wanted most of all. What
remained for such a man to aspire to? There must have been a morning after the
last surrender, when someone drew open his curtains and asked what he wished to
do that day. Someone he feared to disappoint, whose regard he could never bear
to lose. An advisor who genuinely liked his humor. A friend.
A friend would be nice.

Her fingers trailed along the railing,
slowing when she looked over it. A mother crossed the channel below, nothing
but sun-hardened clay to cool her feet. Her son trailed several steps behind,
stopping to examine a dead thing before she called him onward. When he caught
up, she took his hand, and together they climbed the opposite bank.

Had the child ever pictured water
there, or had it always been another road for him, inconveniently deep?

Please let them have enough, she
prayed. Enough that giving some away needn’t leave them thirsty.
paras.html: Please let them have enough, she prayed. Enough that giving some away needn’t leave them thirsty.

paras.text:
She watched until the two disappeared
between the buildings, then closed the widening gap with Evan as the wind
untidied him once again.

Aware of her dissatisfaction, he asked
her, “What is it now?”

“I can’t decide whether I should cut
your hair or leave it as it is.”

“And what happened to my say in the
matter?”

She paid him no heed, already enjoying
her own generosity as she imagined snipping hair away with the scissors in her
bag, forever correcting his posture. “Hold still,” she’d scold him, lifting his
chin, demanding his unbroken attention.

These internal screenplays could last
for hours, but careful scripting required a quieter place, a writing room where
the mind could wander without interruption. She tucked the draft into a drawer
for later. “It’s strong stewardship of you,” she said, “sharing what you have
with helpless animals. Just remember to spare some for Evan too. Even if Evan
can be insensitive.”

“Evan will manage.” He was quiet a
moment, and then he gestured away from the populace. “Don’t go spreading this
around, but the pump at the old baseball field still draws a trickle, if you
keep at it long enough. Rusted to the bolt, though.”

He needed not say more, for he’d
happened upon the girl’s greatest weakness: the relish of trading secrets.
“Prove it,” she said.

Thence he led her through a
neighborhood of brittle shoots and shuttered windows, eventually passing a
ruined petrol station near the edge of town. In the course of this half hour,
they rationed the moisture in their mouths, offering less in the way of small
talk, retreating inward. She took his silence as mutual weariness.

The day grew long, and she felt the
pull toward home, insofar as the word home could be stretched. At least
it offered sanctuary and someone expecting her return. Someone probably deep in
the dark, recounting his silver and arriving at the same intolerable shortage.
If nothing else, he was undoubtedly fretting over her whereabouts, just like
he’d once fretted over her parents, all those many cycles ago.

paras.text:
Recognizing where that trail was
beginning to funnel her, she quickly abandoned it. Mothers. Fathers. Siblings. Never
mind them. Lock away the past before it breaks you.
“Are we almost there?” she asked.
“Just ahead.”

They came to a bend, where bleachers
rose above a broken fence. A squat building stood beside
them, sign dangling on one hinge. Half its lettering had gone, though what
remained hinted of desserts and sweet things, and while she lacked full
understanding of the commissary, she suspected it once offered these upon
request. A bottled soda? Why yes, I’d love one,
please. May I receive it now? Something in that social
tenor.

paras.text:
He lifted a section of sagging fence
to free their path, allowing her to pass beneath. She thanked him and stood at
the other side, taking in the scene in full. The grounds were a far cry from
the orange-blossomed arena of her childhood tournaments. Here, in Historia,
only dust and decay came warm of welcome.

Regrettable, and just the beginning of
her disappointments. She lowered her cowl and turned to face him. “There’s no
water here, is there?”
“There is not.”

The smaller voice within her had
always known, and now she was called to account for ignoring it, for overriding
it in pursuit of companionship.

Remarkable, to be complicit in one’s
own deception, crediting the whole nature of a person by a single kindness.
There were days she thought she’d open the door for the wardens themselves, if
they knocked politely enough.
“I’m sorry,” he told her.

“Then don’t do what you’re
thinking.”

His eyes fell to the satchel,
where her hand had settled over it. “Eleven months I’ve been at it, scraping
for a fare to Crown City, one penny at a time.” He came a step nearer, hand
extended in a gust of wind. “If you really want me to try my luck there, I’ll
need whatever’s in your bag.”

She wanted her uncle with a
suddenness that almost brought her to tears. “I have nothing of value, Evan.”
“I’ll be the judge of that.”

She drew her bag against her side,
still looking at him, waiting, summoning a martial knowledge long stale from
absent practice. There were no orange blossoms here, and there would be no
honor in this engagement.

She evaded his swipe as it came, and
with her right foot secure, the heel of her hand came forward in a thrust
against his chest. He stumbled backward, astonished by the finesse of her
counter-attack.
“Reishotai?” he asked, hesitating.

“I’m warning you! Stay back!” But her
feet had telegraphed her fear, and he followed her retreat. She scrambled
toward the bleachers, finding a groundskeeper’s rake forsaken among them. The
instant her fingers closed around its splintered handle, she swung in an arc so
unreserved that it ripped teeth from his mouth.

The brush was grisly, but it did not
extend far enough to upend him, nor had the pain of the gash begun to bloom.
One hand rose to shield the flap of hanging tissue, and he stood a moment,
attempting to speak. She watched him understand what had been done to him, and
watched the boy who had poured water for a stray go out of him like a candle.

He seized her weapon and flung it
away, driving her to the ground. He was on her then, losing all reason,
striking her incessantly, until all she could do was bear it.

She grew dazed, barely glimpsing the
sunlight failing around his shoulders, his disfigurement, his fist rising
again, and again, his attempts to curse with jaw inert. Blood ran over her own
tongue as she slipped away. Only her fingers continued to plead on her behalf,
gripping his sleeve as though he might help her.

His weight lifted, and the weight of
her satchel went with it. By the sound of his broken chuckle, he’d found the
money upon his rummage, along with the scissors she’d intended for his hair,
and then the chuckle devolved into weeping, into knowing he would no longer eat
as he had eaten, speak as he had spoken. And no one would again look at him the
way she had. The crowns he’d taken would not buy these things back, and yet his
fury demanded someone pay for them.

Somewhere beneath the fog and pain,
she heard his weeping stop, and she urged her body to rise and flee, though it
had already surrendered. Wind carried dust and darkness as it gathered, and
then his boots returned, his weight upon her once again, that together they’d
continue.

“Please, no,” her spirit cried, but to what end? The glint of closed
blades came down just as she managed to bring up her arm to bear them, and
searing pain lanced her beneath the wrist. He reveled in her scream, mindless
to the changing of the sky, deaf to the gale that churned the clouds above
them, soot-black and mightier than a thousand suns.

“Please,” came her naked appeal, even as he raised the scissors
again.

paras.text: “Mama! Save me!”
paras.html: “Mama! Save me!”

paras.text:
Deep within that angry churn, the
matter was decided, and the lightning it sent down threw him across the field
as though he were shot from a cannon, for a pact is not to be trifled with when
it has been made with the Fount. The thunderclap arrived a heartbeat later,
striking the stands into song while he was still in the air. He landed in the
distant outfield, blackened and smoking, and he was no more.

She slipped away, to another time and
place. A grand city. A home in the crystal towers. A kimono as white as snow.
Silky hair, black as India ink. Laughter.

The rumble that rent the firmament had
no end, for that which it heralded has no end. And hushed grew all creation at
the coming of its message, as a household grows still at a father's step.

In the sunless sky above—if anyone
east or west were watching—they’d have caught the outline of the Chrysanthemum
in the clouds, briefly, and gone. Merely the angle of Testament’s solar array,
urges the skeptic, a trick of the light. Not the cosmic proclamation that the
foolish ascribe.

Aluminum bleachers began to stir with
a plink, plink, plink as they were blotted by thick, wet circles.
All throughout the township of Historia, faces began turning upward, people
emerging from doorways to watch their awnings torn away by wind, for watch was
all they could do, as the heavens opened, and the Writ of the Land came at long
last to its welcome end.

paras.text:
Where the girl lay, rain carried
ribbons of red into the soil, which took them gently, and held them in care of
another. Her fingers curled beside her, and she stirred only enough to draw
labored breath. Sayuri was her name, which meant lily in the language of
Kifune, and though I promise you we shall come to know her as we know
ourselves, she is not the central figure in this story.

paras.text:
Nor is the man who found her after
much frantic searching, who’d watched over her since the treachery of their
kinsman, and now grieved at the sight of her wounds. The treasure hoarder
himself, the poor fool she’d stolen from, as Mr. Bodecker had so accurately
described him. Mark was his name.

“I have failed you, my friends. Kaori,
forgive me.”

He lifted sleeping Sayuri in his arms,
and as he did, he understood the shape in the outfield, and was saddened by it.
Then he carried her home in the rising waters, leaving us with the question of
who, then, is most central to our great drama, of who is worthy this honor and
exaltation.

Perhaps, unbeknownst to us, they have
already appeared on the stage. And yet, before we may answer this, we must turn
back time, to a journey through the Sierra Nevada mountains.
II
Shūren

Three years before the waters transformed Historia, a boy lay in the frigid
Sierra Nevada with his father’s bootlace in his fist.

He had ceased to feel the lace some time ago, looking down every so often to
be sure it remained between his fingers before returning his attention to the
raised stone at the edge of the clearing. Beneath it lay a strip of curled
meat, cut from their prior hunt.

At the fallen tree beside him, his father Brent watched the bait,
unblinking. He was so stone still that snow had frosted his shoulders and the
curved blade at his back.

This blade had a name, insisted upon by the wise men of Kifune, as though it
were a name given from on high. Shūren, she was called. A great deal of
importance had been assigned to her by those last remnants, and it could be
said she was the reason his family now starved in the wilderness.

The boy, Noah, knew nothing of such matters. He knew very little, at this
moment, outside the want to stretch his legs, to shake the life back into his
hands. And when the evening turned to night, he glanced again to his father,
who remained exactly as he had been.
A fox appeared between the trees.

It stopped with one forepaw lifted, ears toward the family campfire. Noah
had imagined something meatier while they prepared the trap, yet this creature
looked scarcely better fed than himself.

It sniffed the air, and though its nose had suspicions, desperation was
hardly a position unique to other predators. Sustenance seldom fell randomly
out of the sky, let alone in the dead of winter.

One pull would take the stone’s support away. His father had shown him where
the animal needed to stand, where it would fall and rupture the neck. One pull,
and it would be over before it began. Painless. A soul cleanly released.
The fox padded forward, stopped, then stretched its head toward the bait.

Brent gave the signal, and Noah ripped the prop away. The fox turned, and
their eyes met as the stone crushed its lower flank. Its cry brought Noah
halfway to his feet. Brent had already leapt the crest, drawing a knife and
finishing what should have since been finished. The fox scraped a single bloody
furrow with its paw, and then it was at peace.
Noah stood with the cord still in his grip. He no longer had an appetite.
“Well done,” Brent said at last. “I know it weighs heavy.”

Noah bent to the fallen prop, retrieving the bootlace, wondering if there
was any other lesson to be gained from it all. His father had never been
verbose, and his wisdom was often found in his example as opposed to his
speech. But to his surprise, Brent spoke again.
“Most of what this animal has to offer must go to you and I.”
“But what about mom and Layla?” he asked.

Brent eased the carcass over his shoulder. “They put us first tonight so
that we may have the strength to put them first tomorrow. Your sister does not
invite you to take from her portion unconditionally, lad. You receive it to
maintain your lethality, to defend her always. You must respect this.”

Noah looked at the animal hanging from his father’s shoulder. The night had
grown too cold for further trapping, which meant another night of not having
enough to go around. It was a hard thing to come to terms with, filling his
stomach while Layla sacrificed in silence, but this was his father’s command.
“I understand.”

They followed their tracks through the trees until the campfire showed
between the trunks. Their mother stood at the sound of their return, while
Layla stayed beneath her fur covering. He suspected they'd been earshot of the
slaughter.

Noah stopped between his sister and the fire. “It was quick,” he said. “He
didn’t feel much.”
She drew the fur closer about her knees.
“Next time I can come,” she said.

Noah glanced toward his father, who had seated himself amongst the three of
them.
“I’ll be tough,” Layla promised. “I won’t cry, daddy. I can come.”

“You certainly could, Layla. But then who would tend to your duties at
camp?  Do you think your brother would do a fine job? Or would we come
home to a disaster?”

“I’d rather not say,” she said, throwing Noah a teasing smile. She lifted an
edge of her fur for Noah, who sat beside her. He was keen to accept it, and did
not worry himself for a rebuttal.

Across from them, their mother’s hand had come to rest on Brent’s shoulder.
He covered it with his own.
“Give me a moment,” he told her.

She nodded, then set about dressing the animal. Noah watched his father
stretch his hands toward the flames.

By the time supper was ready, hunger had returned to Noah. The meat was
leathery and wild, but he ate the portion given him.

Afterward he took first watch without being asked, sitting with his back to
the fire and his eyes upon the trees. The cold had seeped halfway through his
feet when a tremor passed beneath them, deep enough to trouble the pebbles by
his ankles. The third in as many days. He glanced toward Layla, who was licking
grease from her fingers, oblivious.

When he turned back to the forest, he replayed the moment the fox had looked
at him, and he offered silent apology.

He had been watching the same opening between the trees for some time,
though he couldn't have said what had passed through it. His focus was
elsewhere.

“If you’re keeping watch over something that’s already happened,” his mother
said, “you might as well go do it beside the fire.”
He looked up as she stepped beside him, brushing hair from his forehead.
“My turn," she said.
“I can stay a little longer.”
“No. Go warm yourself.”

Noah rose, working the stiffness from his knees before returning to the
fire. His father had settled against a tree, Layla beneath his arm. She was
watching the branches overhead, where ravens disputed amongst themselves. A
gust shook pine needles from their perches and sent a fresh round of complaints
through the trees.
“Go away!” Layla called.
“Leave them be, sweetheart. They’ll settle down soon enough.”
“They’re keeping everyone awake.”
“You might set them an example.”

She buried her face inside his coat as Noah sat on his father’s other side.
He'd scarcely felt the wind on his watch, but now it seemed to find every
opening in his clothes.
“People always like you, dad. Why can’t we ask someone for help?”

“We have the girls to think of before we ask a stranger for kindness. Your
mother spent years as the unofficial face of the Realm. The woman was an icon,
even beyond our borders. No, son, there's nowhere we can go she won’t be
recognized.”
“But the Realm is gone.”
Brent looked toward Elizabeth’s place among the trees.
“Yes,” he said. “It is.”
Layla shifted against him, snoring gently.

Noah waited, but his father offered nothing more. He turned away, drawing
the fur over his shoulder and finding a place to rest his head. Somewhere among
the branches a raven made one final objection to their presence.

His eyes closed. For a while he could still hear his father breathing, which
calmed him. When sleep came, he was transported to a memory of his mother
crossing over carpet so extravagant that her footsteps made no sound. He kept
pace while she fastened the last button at her wrist. Through the windows of
their corridor, the Realm’s spaceport of Sungarde glittered in the mists of the
Niagara Falls.

She stole one final look at her compact and then looked back to make certain
he was coming.

Of course he was coming. He'd been living in anticipation of this, his debut
semi-final in the Realm's official combat sport.

Reishotai no Youni, it was called. As the Script. A mixed martial art
that had long been guarded by the elders of Kifune, and a secret the Council
eventually acquired through ceaseless goodwill. Mostly. A modified version of
the original Script was permitted to be imported, one which did not remove agency
from non-practitioners.

paras.text:
By the time they reached the arena, the afternoon had warmed the tatami
beneath his tabi socks. Banners of the Eight-Point Chrysanthemum stirred above
the spectators, and orange blossoms scented the air. Somewhere in that crowd
his father would be finding their seats, Layla on his shoulders for a better
view.
Noah tightened his grip upon the wooden practice katana.

Across from him, a girl waited with her naginata. She was younger than him
by a year or two, which surprised him until she took her stance. The symbol of
House Hirata had been embroidered upon her reishogi, which was not a thing you
wanted to see. What he had over her in mass, she more than reclaimed in
pedigree. He was so outclassed that he should have been angry.
She held her naginata steady between them. He adjusted his grip.
“Contestants,” the marshal called. “Approach. Bow.”

They stepped to their marks and obeyed the command. When she straightened, a
strand of walnut hair had slipped across her cheek. She blew it aside without
taking her eyes from him.

He heard his mother call his name from the stands. There she was beside his
father, waving as though he might have forgotten which mother was his. Layla
waved both hands. He wished they would stop.
Their adjudicator stepped clear.

At the signal, Noah advanced, testing her reach with a strike she turned
aside. He changed his angle, and the shaft of her lance caught his practice
blade with a crack that carried into the stands. Before he could recover, she
touched his ribs.
“Point.”
Applause.

The girl withdrew to her mark, and Noah to his own. He caught the ferocity
in her gaze and chuckled despite himself. Setting his pride to the left, he
found he was quite enjoying the present company.

She offered another opening, but he opted instead for her weapon, disarming
her. His left foot answered her open-hand strike, exposing her posterior to a
swat with his blade.
“Point.”

The girl inspected the place he’d struck, as though she’d been party to some
impropriety. Noah thought it best to occupy himself with retrieving her
naginata.

She accepted the weapon, but not his courtesy. “I’ll never forgive you for
that.”
“You’ll hate me forever?” he asked, and remained unacknowledged.

(Forgive me, friends. Such declarative banter among rivals and future
companions brings a tear to your chronicler’s eye!)

They took longer over the deciding point. He’d begun recognizing the small
movements that preceded her attacks, though recognizing them and evading them
proved separate challenges. When he finally caught her across the middle, he
was short of breath.
The marshal raised his hand. “Match. Burnfield.”

He drew back, surprised to find it over. From the stands came his mother’s
uninhibited victory cry, followed by Layla’s attempt to eclipse it.
The girl bowed. “Omedetou gozaimasu,” she said.

Noah drank from a water bottle as he watched her leave, and it came to him
then, that there went a girl he’d have liked to get to know.
He woke with his cheek against the root and his parents somewhere near.
“All well?” his father asked.
“All well.”

Noah shifted beneath the fur. Layla had found him in the midst of the night,
and he drew the covering over her shoulder before looking after himself. By
then the dream had all but slipped beyond recall. He tried to remember who had
won the match, to remember the grudge he’d incurred that day, but all he could
remember was the lightning in her eyes.
Then he slept again.

Now that this brief introduction is
finished, I speak to you directly, my Good Council.

You have indulged me for these past two years, and some of you have been
kept waiting on the finalization of this work for over a decade. I think we can
all agree that I have spoken of it long enough. However, there are a few final
matters I would like to address before I turn my focus to the next chapter of polish
and delivery.
On Legality.

Some of you, with the love and good sense that only old friends bring to
such conversations, have urged me to change the names in this book, to protect
myself, if I were to pursue publication. You were not wrong to suggest as much,
and a more prudent man would have taken your advice without further discussion.

I have made my peace with what this means in practical terms: I will not be
courting agents who would require me to censor the story, and I have no
interest in erasing the people I love from this work in pursuit of personal
success. If this book finds the wider world in my lifetime, I will be pleased.
But if not, the book will still exist, waiting for the right reader to find it
long after the empire has forgotten us. I do not need to see it handed to them.

You who urged me toward safety did so out of love, and I received it as
love.

It is also out of love that I must refuse. Whatever happens to it, and to
me, our people will be in it, named and known, exactly as we have always been.
That is the only version of this story I ever desired to tell. And perhaps, now
that we’ve arrived here, you will also agree that anything lesser would be heartbreaking.
On Gratitude.

Some debts are too great to summarize, but a final letter is where one
tries.

There was a grandmother who read the immature writings of a teenage grandson
and saw something like Covenant in them. There were English teachers who agreed
with her. From that belief came the deep foundation. Everything that followed
was built on top of it.

Then came the season of summer, surrounded by a particular ensemble cast:
The kind that does not appear in life twice, and the kind that I did not fully
understand was finite and beautiful. Later, an envelope on a desk in Japan,
waiting for me to return from one of life’s adventures. Inside it was a
newsletter detailing the recent days of our Council, a gift from my very best
friend, who thought I might want to know how things were going back home. And
so our lore began.

Further issues of High Council News arrived in mailboxes, but even then, we
understood an important truth: The most special things have an end.

That was until I laid eyes on my little girl for the first time, and
suddenly I knew that our story had not finished. I began speaking of a
continuation to the saga, which was met with incredible enthusiasm from the
very face of the Realm herself. Then came the excitement of those who arrived
later, who never knew of our Council, and who have nothing invested in this
story except their investment in me. They’ve cheered me on without
understanding what they were cheering for, only hoping that it pushed me on.
It did. Alberto, Kirsten, Justin, Grace, Krash.

I can’t think of any fellow Civilization VI players to mention. At least not
any good ones.

And finally, the people who have actually borne the manuscript, who have
read it in its roughest forms and called it the ugly baby that it was, and kept
reading anyway. My brother, mother, and incredible partner. My fellow aspiring
authors. I cannot pay any of you back. I can only show you what I made with
what you gave me, and hope you find yourself inside it.
On the Future.

A few of you have wondered if Covenant is only the beginning. If a sequel
might be possible.
The honest answer is no.

This is the story I have set out to tell, and I do not believe I would ever
be able to top it.

At the same time, there are corners of this world I’ve left unexplored,
characters I wish I could spend far more time with. Some of you in my
confidence have already fallen in love with certain Imperial-aligned
personalities and are now quite insistent on a satellite novella. I am open to
these possibilities, but I won’t force them.
Perhaps I’ll leave the decision with you, my co-authors since the beginning.
Conclusion:

The posturing is over. The book is what comes next, along with its
continuation of Chapter II. It will take longer than I have historically
predicted, for I do not possess any particular innate talent in writing. I
struggle through it for another reason. Thank you for your patience, and may
the Eight-Point endure eternal.
Your Citadel Chronicler
